nameStory: The 'ciliate' in this lichen's name comes from the Latin word for 'eyelash,' referring to the tiny hair-like projections along the edges of its lobes that look like delicate fringe. The 'wreath' part describes how the circular, rosette-like growth pattern resembles a decorative wreath when viewed from above. Together, it's like nature's own fringed holiday decoration!
description: Ciliate Wreath Lichen is a small, flat lichen that grows in neat circular patches resembling tiny wreaths on tree bark and rocks. The grayish-green body forms overlapping lobes that radiate outward from the center, typically reaching only 1-3 inches across. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together: a fungus and an algae working as partners to survive in harsh conditions. The distinctive 'eyelash' fringe around each lobe makes it stand out from other small crusty lichens.

idTips.label: Fringed edges
idTips.description: Look for tiny white to pale brown hair-like projections along the lobe edges that feel slightly rough when gently touched with a fingertip, like microscopic bristles

idTips.label: Circular growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms neat rosettes or wreaths typically 1-3 inches across, with lobes radiating outward from a central point like spokes on a wheel

idTips.label: Gray-green color
idTips.description: Surface appears dusty gray-green to brownish-gray, often with a slightly powdery texture that may rub off on your fingers when touched

idTips.label: Overlapping lobes
idTips.description: Individual lobes overlap like shingles, creating a layered appearance with slightly raised edges that cast small shadows

idTips.label: Substrate preference
idTips.description: Almost always found growing on tree bark, particularly favoring rough-barked trees where it can grip firmly to vertical surfaces

habitat: Look for Ciliate Wreath Lichen on the bark of deciduous trees, especially those with rough, furrowed bark like oaks, maples, and ash trees. It prefers partially shaded locations in forests, parks, and along woodland edges where air quality is relatively good. This lichen is quite rare in New England, so check older trees in less polluted areas away from busy roads.

seasonality.spring: Most visible after winter moisture has helped the lichen expand and become more pliable. The grayish-green color appears more vibrant against fresh spring bark.
seasonality.summer: May appear somewhat shrunken and darker during dry periods, with the fringed edges becoming more brittle and prominent as the lichen contracts.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most visible as falling leaves expose more bark surface, and autumn moisture helps the lichen plump up and show better color contrast.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but may appear flatter and more muted in color. Snow and ice can actually help preserve the lichen during harsh weather.

funFact: This tiny lichen can live for decades or even centuries, slowly growing outward at a rate of less than a millimeter per year - meaning that 2-inch specimen you're looking at could be older than your great-grandparents!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small gray lichens, but the distinctive white 'eyelashes' along the lobe edges are your key - run your finger gently around the edges and you'll feel those tiny bristles that other similar species lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Shadow Lichens' in their scientific group name, these lichens actually prefer moderate light conditions rather than deep shade - the 'shadow' refers more to their often subtle, muted coloring that can blend into bark patterns.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Ciliate Wreath Lichen is the only one with prominent white hair-like projections along all lobe edges. Other wreath lichens like Mealy Shadow Lichen may have powdery surfaces but lack the distinctive fringe, while Hairy Shadow Lichen has scattered hairs on the surface rather than organized edge bristles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Orange-cored Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its bright orange pycnidial contents - most other wreath lichens in this genus have white, yellow, or red cores instead.
Among the shadow lichens in its genus, Pom-pom Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its small size and abundant powdery soredia clusters.
Among its wreath lichen relatives, Powder-tipped Shadow Lichen is distinguished by having the white soredia concentrated specifically at the lobe tips rather than scattered across the surface.
Among its relatives, Hairy Shadow Lichen is distinguished by those characteristic hair-like edge projections that other shadow lichens lack.
Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Dark Shadow Lichen is easily recognized by its abundant black isidia that cover both the center and edges of the lobes.

Unlike its relatives such as Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange inner tissues) or Hairy Shadow Lichen (which has fuzzy edges), Mealy Shadow Lichen lacks both colorful internal tissues and hairy margins.

Unlike its relatives like Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange interiors) or Mealy Shadow Lichen (which has white powdery surfaces), Red-cored Starburst Shadow Lichen is the only species in its genus with the distinctive crimson interior.
Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Whiskered Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its particularly prominent marginal cilia and small size.
Among its shadow lichen relatives, Scaly Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its prominently curled, squarrose lobes that create a three-dimensional texture.
